recent_posts.title: Setting up testcontainers for Ruby on Rails testing
recent_posts.summary: Testcontainers is an open-source library that provides throwaway, lightweight Docker containers for testing dependencies like databases and Redis. Instead of installing PostgreSQL or Redis locally, you can spin up versioned containers that match your production environment, avoiding version mismatches between local, CI, and production. The tutorial demonstrates setting up Testcontainers in a Ruby on Rails project with RSpec, configuring PostgreSQL and Redis containers that automatically start before tests and clean up afterward. This approach ensures consistent testing environments and prevents issues caused by dependency version differences.

recent_posts.title: Setting up Framework Desktop for AI hosting and gaming on Linux
recent_posts.summary: The Framework Desktop with AMD Ryzen AI Max 395 chipset and 128GB unified RAM excels at Linux development, local AI model hosting, and gaming. The unified memory architecture allows the integrated GPU to leverage all available RAM. A detailed walkthrough covers assembling the machine, installing Arch Linux with Omari window manager, setting up Ollama for local AI models, configuring OpenCode as a coding agent frontend, exposing AI models over the network using Enrok tunneling, and gaming performance with Path of Exile 2 on Steam with Vulkan drivers.

recent_posts.title: Getting started with Yazi terminal file browser
recent_posts.summary: Yazi is a terminal-based file browser built in Rust that enables keyboard-driven file management. It supports vim-style navigation, file previews (including images, videos, and compressed files), fuzzy finding with FZF integration, bulk operations like copying and renaming multiple files, and customizable themes. Available across Linux, macOS, and Windows, it offers a faster alternative to GUI file managers for developers comfortable with terminal workflows.

recent_posts.title: You installed Omarchy, Now What?
recent_posts.summary: A practical guide to customizing Omarchy (an Arch Linux + Hyperland configuration) after installation. Covers creating idempotent shell scripts to automate program installation, managing dotfiles with GNU Stow, and overriding default configurations. Demonstrates the entire workflow by setting up a fresh installation on a Framework 13 laptop, showing how to make configurations portable and reproducible across multiple machines.

recent_posts.title: How to safely verify bash scripts before execution
recent_posts.summary: Installing packages via curl-to-bash commands poses security risks. Two methods help verify script safety: saving the script to a file for manual inspection before execution, and validating checksums using SHA-256 to detect unauthorized modifications. These practices prevent accidentally running malicious code on your system.

recent_posts.title: Setting up Omarchy tiling window manager on Arch Linux
recent_posts.summary: Omarchy is a preconfigured Arch Linux setup with Hyperland tiling window manager that simplifies the traditionally complex process of setting up a tiling window manager environment. The setup includes theme switching, application launching, status bar, notifications, and various preconfigured tools like Waybar, Neovim with LazyVim, and Bluetooth management. Installation requires only one command after installing Arch Linux, and the entire configuration is built using transparent shell scripts that are easily extensible. The project aims to make Linux tiling window managers more accessible to newcomers by providing an opinionated but well-configured starting point.

recent_posts.title: From gaming machines to Linux and programming
recent_posts.summary: A personal reflection on how building gaming machines can lead to deeper interests in Linux, tiling window managers, and programming. The author encourages embracing curiosity about computing and staying open to new possibilities that might spark passion for technology.

recent_posts.title: Embrace your genuine enthusiasm for computers and technology
recent_posts.summary: Embracing genuine enthusiasm for computers and technology leads to better learning outcomes and creates infectious excitement within communities. The Linux community particularly benefits from authentic passion, as people who openly enjoy what they do inspire others to explore and discover new technologies without irony or reservation.

recent_posts.title: Learning Linux takes less time than your weekly social media scrolling
recent_posts.summary: The perceived difficulty of learning Linux is often exaggerated when compared to the time people spend on unproductive activities like social media scrolling. Setting up even complex Linux distributions like Arch with Hyperland takes 30-50 hours total, which equals just 2-3 weeks of typical daily social media usage. The investment in learning Linux provides long-term benefits and improved computing experience, making it a worthwhile trade-off compared to passive screen time.

recent_posts.title: Three practical uses for the Linux yes command
recent_posts.summary: The Linux 'yes' command continuously prints a string until terminated, offering practical applications beyond its seemingly odd behavior. It serves as a useful tool for process management practice, generating large test files quickly, and automating script installations by automatically responding 'yes' to prompts when piped to other commands.

top_posts.title: Managing Docker efficiently with lazy Docker
top_posts.summary: Managing Docker containers and images can be simplified with a tool called lazy Docker. Created by Jesse Duffield, it offers a terminal UI that helps users perform Docker commands with ease. This tool allows you to manage containers, images, volumes, and networks through a clean and efficient terminal interface. Instructions for installation on different operating systems, such as Mac, Windows, and others, are provided. It’s useful for those who often forget Docker commands or prefer working within the terminal.

Learn how to create and execute scripts for package installations and system configurations, making your Linux environment reproducible and flexible. top_posts.title: Setting up a thin client development environment with VPS and secure remote access
top_posts.summary: A thin client development setup allows developers to work from any device by connecting to a powerful VPS server. The setup involves provisioning a VPS (like Digital Ocean), installing development tools, and using secure connection services like Border Zero to avoid exposing SSH ports. This approach enables coding from tablets, old laptops, or any device while maintaining a consistent development environment with tools like tmux and neovim running on the remote server.

top_posts.title: 10 surprising things you can do with Vim
top_posts.summary: Discover 10 quirky but impressive tricks you can do with Vim, from ROT13 encryption and inserting random data to browsing web content and converting files to HTML. These tips showcase some fun and lesser-known features of Vim that can either be practical or just amusing. Join in to expand your Vim knowledge and impress your peers.
